title: Month 21
subtitle: Running, kicking, and climbing. The body is ahead of the words, and that is the right order.

baby.development: Your child runs well, can kick a ball forward, and walks up stairs with a hand held. They say around fifty words and are starting to put two together.

you.body: If you are pregnant again, twenty-one months is the age gap where the lifting gets hard. Ask for help rather than pushing through.
you.mind: Twenty-one months is often when the child starts to help. Let them, even when it is slower.

coreActions.title: Let them help, even when it is slower
coreActions.why: Helping is how a child learns to be part of a household, and the willingness to help peaks before the ability.
coreActions.detail: Put the laundry in the basket together. Hand them a cloth to wipe the table. Let them stir. It takes three times as long and it is the whole point. A child who helps at two is a child who helps at four.

coreActions.title: Kick and roll a ball every day
coreActions.why: Kicking a ball is a balance and coordination skill, and it is the foundation for running, jumping, and sport.
coreActions.detail: Roll a ball back and forth sitting down first, then standing. Kick a soft ball indoors. A child who can kick forward at two is on track. Do not correct the foot, just play.

coreActions.title: Know the water rules before summer
coreActions.why: Drowning is the leading cause of injury death in children one to four, and it is silent.
coreActions.detail: A child this age needs an adult within arm's reach in any water, including a bathtub and a paddling pool. Empty the paddling pool after every use. A fence with a self-closing gate around a pool is the thing that works.

alsoKnow.title: Two words is enough for now
alsoKnow.body: Two-word phrases between eighteen and twenty-four months are on track. Three words usually come between twenty-four and thirty months. A child with no two-word phrases at twenty-four months is worth raising at the visit.

alsoKnow.title: One nap is the norm now
alsoKnow.body: Most children are on one nap by twenty-one months, usually after lunch, for one to two hours. A child who still needs two is not behind.

redFlags.text: A child missing near water, or found face down in water
Choking — cannot breathe, cough, or make a sound
A fever over 100.4°F with unusual sleepiness or a rash
